- **extended** (ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Ch 4 Dramani-Issifou)): Gold producers kept their own religion: al-Umari (fourteenth century) says the Mansa of Mali exempted populations who kept traditional religions from the tax on unbelievers, because they worked the gold mines. The gold producers were not converted and were very numerous. Use in the Mali lesson: the gold was the reason for religious tolerance, and the Muslim middlemen depended on it.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Ch 4 Dramani-Issifou)): Blacksmiths and kingship: in many areas royal power was bound up with master smiths, whose magic made them feared. As Islam took hold, the smiths were pushed out of politics, became an isolated group, and were later treated as a caste. The volume reads the Sundiata-Sumaoro story as a clash over this alliance, with Sundiata an ironmaster who would not yield to the traditional religion's pressure. Use in the Mali and Sundiata lessons.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Ch 4 Dramani-Issifou)): Islam before the sixth/twelfth century spread without wars or forced conversion, through princes and merchants, and its advances were not irreversible. Muslim merchants lived in minority quarters near royal cities, with their own mosques, and were probably exempt from some taxes. Use in the Ghana and Mali lessons on Muslim quarters.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt chunk 3 (Ch 4 Dramani-Issifou)): Askiya Muhammad's consultations: after his coup, Askiya Muhammad of Songhai made the pilgrimage (about AD 1497), was given the title of caliph, and asked four consultations from al-Ansamani, al-Suyuti and al-Maghili on inheritance and social questions. Al-Maghili wrote a handbook of the perfect Muslim prince. Use in the Songhai lesson on the jurists' role at court.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt chunk 3 (Ch 4 Dramani-Issifou)): Ancestral rites kept by Muslim rulers: the Mali emperors kept the drum, the sacred fire, the rules of dress and the high priest of ancestors and spirits (Hori Farima). Askiya Muhammad also kept these, despite the jurists' advice, and Ibn Dunama's Bornu kept its mai as a living god with learned imams at court. Use in the Mali, Songhai and Bornu lessons: rulers kept the old power forms.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt chunk 3 (Ch 4 Dramani-Issifou)): Results of pressure from jurists: in Katsina, after al-Maghili's visit, sacred groves were cut down and mosques built, but the changes did not last. Notables in Bornu refused the imams' moral rules. Use in the Hausa lesson on how far reform reached.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt chunk 4 (Ch 4 Dramani-Issifou)): Sonni Ali's counter-offensive: Sonni Ali of Songhay (AD 1464-1492) turned on the Muslim scholars of Timbuktu, whom he saw as foreigners challenging his magic kingship; the Timbuktu-Gao conflict followed, and Askiya Muhammad's coup of 1493 made Islam the state's option. Use in the Songhai and Timbuktu lessons: the anti-Muslim reaction came from a king, not from the masses.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt chunk 4 (Ch 4 Dramani-Issifou)): Moroccan conquest and retreat: after the Moroccan conquest of the 1590s the Songhai cities declined, people moved south into Dendi, and the Bambara kingdom of Segu emerged as an animist state in the seventeenth century, after the collapse of Muslim imperial power. Use in the late Songhai and Segu lessons.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt chunk 4 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): Zanj revolt and African labour: the Zanj revolt in Iraq (AD 869-883, with African slave labour in the salt marshes) ended large-scale slave plantation labour in the Muslim east, led to the rise of feudal production, and hardened racial contempt for black Africans in Muslim writing. Use in the slave trade and Swahili lessons on how the revolt changed the demand for slaves.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Part II, Hrbek)): Ghana's Islamisation was not by conquest: the chapter says the Almoravid conquest of Ghana usually cited as the model is not supported by the available evidence, and external conquest played little role south of the Sahara except in the eastern Sudan. Use in the Ghana lesson on 'Did the Almoravids conquer Ghana in 1076?': this chapter supports the lesson's sceptical reading.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Part II, Hrbek)): Ibadite trade and mission in the Sudan: Ibadite merchants from Tahert, Wargla, southern Tunisia and Jabal Nafusa settled in Ghana, Gao, Awdaghust, Tadmekka and Ghaylan, and the Ibadite Banu Khattab held the Fezzan end of the Libya-Chad route. Ibadites reached the Sudan before orthodox Sunnis and may have made some of the first converts. Minaret forms and minbars in the Sudan follow Tunisian and Mzab Ibadite models. Use in the early Islam and Sudan lessons, with the source gaps marked.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Part II, Hrbek)): Islam came first to towns and rulers: merchants and clerics formed Muslim quarters with their own shaykhs and qadis in trading cities, and clerics offered healing, divination and charms. Early rulers were converted: Waar Dyabe of Takrur before the 1030s, Kosoy of Gao around AD 1009-10, and the king of Mallal, whose conversion followed a rain prayer; the courts kept traditional ceremony. Use in the Ghana, Gao and Mallal lessons: a royal conversion is not the people's.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Part II, Hrbek)): Islam and trade: Hopkins's account holds that Islam's ethics gave merchants a shared code, trust and credit across scattered communities, which is why the Dyula, Hausa and Dyakhanke traders were among the first converts. Use in the Dyula and Hausa lessons as the trade-based explanation of conversion.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Part II, Hrbek)): Reasons for state Islam: the rulers of the Sudanese empires used Islam for trade ties with North African partners, to bind subject clans with a common religion, and for Muslim scribes; Muslim clerics at court prepared the conversions of the rulers, who still kept pagan rites. Use in the Mali, Songhai and Bornu lessons as the state's motives for conversion.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Part II, Hrbek)): A clerical class of Sudanese origin: by the fourteenth century the judges, imams and khatibs of Timbuktu were black Muslims from the interior, and many had studied in Fez. The chapter says from then on Islam was carried by Africans who knew the languages and customs, and so became an African religion. Use in the Timbuktu and Mali lessons on the rise of African scholars.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Part II, Hrbek)): Mixed Islam in the Sudan: al-Suyuti's letter to Ibrahim Sara of Katsina (Gobir) reports people who sacrificed a slave to save the sick. Court circles were only superficially Muslim while the masses kept their faith; the chapter calls the result 'mixed' Islam. Use in the Hausa and Gobir lessons.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Part II, Hrbek)): Senegambia and Bornu: by about AD 1500 most Gambian peoples were Muslim, and clerics called bixirim by the Portuguese spread the faith from three ribats on the Gambia; Bornu became Muslim under Hummay, with Dunama's pilgrimage and drowning. Use in the Senegambia and Bornu lessons.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Part II, Hrbek)): The Funj and the Nilotic Sudan: Sufi missionaries converted the Funj, a dark-skinned people from the upper Blue Nile, and by about AD 1500 the southern limit of Islam was set along the 13th parallel. Arabisation went with it, and the Gezira and Kordofan were settled by Arab nomads. Use in the Funj and Sennar lessons.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): The white-origin theme is late: al-Bakri (before 1068) says Ghana was ruled by a black pagan king, and the white-origin account first appears with al-Idrisi in the twelfth century, after the Almoravid intervention. Oral traditions of white first rulers were recorded centuries later and project present relations back. Use in the Ghana lesson as the date at which the theme enters the sources.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): The Fulani: the chapter places their origin in southern Mauritania, with Fulfulde showing an African substratum close to Wolof and Serer, and their movement to the Senegal Valley, Futa Toro, Diomboko and Kaarta, Masina and Futa Jallon was slow and not invasions. The Hamitic and Nubian or Indian origins it lists are not supported. Use in the Fulani and Tukulor lessons; the ethnonym Tukulor is a colonial label.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): Soninke dispersal: after a seven-year drought, the Wagadu people fled south, and some Soninke stayed in Awkar and Hodh and founded ancient Ghana. The chapter says the migration took centuries and is not reconstructed in a firm chronology. Use in the Soninke and Ghana lessons: climate as the probable driver, with the timing open.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): Ghana's power over Awdaghust: from about AD 990 Ghana dominated Awdaghust through the Zanata, and a century later the Almoravids weakened that primacy. The chapter says tension between the Berbers and the black states did not make the Berbers take the states over, because the states had built their own organisation. Use in the Ghana and Almoravid lessons: the states' strength, not Berber conquest.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): Iron and horses made the states: iron gave military superiority and horses and camels gave mobility, and the chapter links blacksmiths' power in oral tradition with the rise of Kanem and Ghana. Use in the state-formation lessons: name iron and mobility as the two material bases in the volume's view.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): Ghana's trade tax and monopoly: al-Bakri says traders paid one dinar on salt coming in and two on salt going out, and the king kept all gold nuggets to keep the price up. The chapter reads Ghana as the hub that distributed salt and took gold for it, and says the Libyo-Berber traders did not introduce that system. Use in the Ghana trade lesson: the tax and the monopoly are the case for Ghana's own control.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): Sacred kingship in Ghana and Gao: al-Bakri describes the Ghana king's sewn robes, gilded cap, subjects throwing earth on their heads (Muslims only clapped), and royal funerals with servants buried and sacred woods. At Gao, the meal was marked by drums and shouts. The chapter treats this sacred kingship as indigenous, not diffused from Egypt. Use in the Ghana and Gao lessons on court ritual.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): Islam limited the slave trade: in Kanem the Sefuwa took power when the country became Muslim, but it was forbidden to enslave a free Muslim, so their economy, based on the slave trade, had to adapt. Use in the Kanem and slave-trade lessons: religion changed what could be sold.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): Ghana's Muslim town: al-Bakri describes a Muslim quarter beside the king's town with twelve mosques, each with its imam, muezzin and reader, and Muslim lawyers and scholars; Muslims were not obliged to follow customs incompatible with their faith. Use in the Ghana lesson on Muslim quarters, with al-Bakri as the source.
- **extended** (ch-015.txt chunk 1 (Ch 12 Talbi)): The Fatimid interest in the Maghrib was the western gold route: the Zanata controlled the caravan terminals towards Lake Chad and Gao, and the Fatimids tried to tap Sudanese gold through Sijilmasa. The chapter says the control of the gold route, not colonising the Maghrib, was the chief aim. Use in the Sudan gold lesson (module 4 link), attributing to Talbi and noting that Devisse and Cahen developed the point.
- **extended** (ch-031.txt chunk 1 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Trade towns: Sijilmasa, founded about 757 from a nomad camel fair in Tafilalt, was the main transSaharan staging post until the eleventh century; Awdaghust was the Sanhaja market linking the Sudan with Barbary; Ghana/Kumbi Saleh, Silla, Yaresi on the Senegal and Kawkaw on the Niger linked the savanna and forest. Use in the Sahara trade lesson (module 4 link).
- **extended** (ch-031.txt chunk 1 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Horses and trade: the trade in Arab barbs (Barbary horses) to the savanna, where trypanosomiasis did not kill horses, led to the decline of the smaller local pony by the eleventh century. Numidia and Nubia bred the Barbary horses for export to the Western and Central Sudan. Use in the Sudan trade and horse lesson.
- **extended** (ch-031.txt chunk 1 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Subsistence and luxury trade: Maghrib wheat went by caravan via Sijilmasa to the western Sahara and Sudan; Biskra supplied up to 1000 camel-loads a day in good years (al-Bakri); salt from Taghaza sold at 200-300 dinars a camel-load (Ibn Hawqal). Use in the Sahara trade economics lesson.
- **extended** (ch-031.txt chunk 1 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Gold producers, in decreasing importance: Bambuk/Galam and Bure in West Africa, southern Africa, and Nubia. Copper circulated as rings currency at Silla and was traded from Katanga, Air and the western Sahara to Yorubaland and North Africa. Use in the gold and copper lesson with the source list.
- **extended** (ch-031.txt chunk 2 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Agriculture: the foggara (stone-lined underground irrigation channels) in the Maghrib and Saharan oases allowed rice, cotton and sugar cane. The walled and terraced Gangara fields of Assaba (Mauritania) probably date from the Almoravid period. Rice from Asia reached the Egyptian oases; sorghum spread from Africa to Egypt, Cyrenaica and even Syria. Use in the agriculture lesson with these sites.
- **extended** (ch-031.txt chunk 2 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Paper: the manufacture of paper from flax, then cotton, on the Chinese model, from the end of the tenth century, replaced parchment and papyrus and broadened intellectual life. Sfax's pressing methods came from Alexandria (al-Bakri). Use in the crafts and technology lesson.
- **extended** (ch-031.txt chunk 2 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Conversion at the courts: in Ghana the emperor chose interpreters and most ministers from the Muslims; in Gao no one reigned without conversion; a Mali king was converted in the eleventh century after a Muslim's prayers supposedly ended a drought; the king of Takrur, War Diabi, was a Muslim proselytiser. Use in the Sudan states lesson (module 4), attributed to al-Bakri.
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 1 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Desert power shift: from the third century, camel breeders and route controllers took over the Sahara; its Berber-speaking peoples revived in the tenth and eleventh centuries as Muslim states wanted gold. This is the background to the Almoravid movement. Use in the Sahara lesson (module 4 and Almoravids).
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 2 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Gold production: alluvial panning in West Africa, Nubia and later Zimbabwe; gold from the West African forest was already going north by about 1100; demand grew in the tenth and eleventh centuries. Mines on the Zimbabwe plateau are attested archaeologically, and a fourteenth-century source (al-Umari, quoting Mansa Musa) describes pit mines. The editors think mining may have begun in the tenth century, but say this is not proven. Use in the gold lesson; mark the mining date as open.
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 3 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Cotton and cloth: cotton was in the Senegal floodplain villages by the tenth century; narrow-strip cloth of the tenth and eleventh centuries comes from the Tellem caves; cotton weaving was in Ethiopia and southern Mozambique by about 900. The narrow two-heddle loom came in before 1000, perhaps from the Nile Valley. Use in the textile lesson with these sites.
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 3 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Salt: rock salt bars from Sahel and East African mines, sea and lagoon salt, and plant-ash salt; salt was currency in Ethiopia at times, and the Sahara exchanged its salt for Sahel grain. Salt from Idjil was carried in caravans. Use in the salt and food lesson.
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 3 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Trans-Saharan trade: classic system of gold and food north for salt and manufactures south; from about 800 a dramatic increase; Igbo-Ukwu received thousands of beads in the ninth century; by about 1100 the trade reached the forest edge of the later Gold Coast. The chapter says trans-Saharan trade drove the development of state institutions from Morocco to Egypt, and across the Sahel from the Atlantic to Lake Chad, in the eighth to eleventh centuries. Use in the trans-Saharan trade and state lesson.
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 4 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Christian Nubia's trade: two economies, one subsistence farming, the other a trade with Muslim merchants who supplied the court with cloth, wine and grain in exchange for slaves; the slaves came from the Chad basin and areas south of Nubia (Nubian pottery in Darfur and Koro Toro supports this). The Fatimid envoy al-Uswani does not mention these links. Use in the Nubia trade lesson.
- **note** (ch-014 chunk 4 (Lewicki, Wargla and Sadrata)): Wargla (Warkilan) and its capital Sadrata were Ibadite oases; the last Rustumid imam Yaqub fled there after Tahert fell; Sadrata was besieged in 934 and abandoned. Wargla was the start of the route to the Western Sudan. Module 4 can use it as an example of Ibadite trade communities.
- **note** (ch-017 chunk 2 (Devisse, Egyptian route to Kawar)): Devisse: the Egyptian route through Kawar and Marandet (Gao) was in use in the ninth century, was dismissed as too dangerous by Ibn Hawkal in the tenth, and fell out of the sources. The Nubian bakt delivered several hundred slaves a year to Egypt. Useful for Module 4 on eastern routes.
- **note** (ch-017 chunk 7 (Devisse, Awdaghust and Kumbi Saleh)): Devisse: Awdaghust was a big town in the 10th and 11th centuries with a break around the mid-11th century; Kumbi Saleh (Ghana) has occupation layers from the 8th to the 15th centuries, more than seven metres deep, and a major mosque; the royal capital al-Bakri describes has not been found. Module 4 can say that archaeology confirms a long urban history but not yet the royal capital.
- **note** (ch-017 chunk 7 (Devisse, Jenne-Jeno and the Sahel)): Devisse: Jenne-Jeno was a town from about 400 to 900 and grew again from 900 to 1400, and Begho had activity from the 2nd century; these sites make West Africa less a dependency of the north than the older picture implied. Module 4 should give this as the Sahel background to Ghana.
- **note** (ch-017 chunk 9 (Devisse, mud architecture)): Devisse: mud architecture predates the trans-Saharan trade; Tegdaoust and Kumbi Saleh used stone for their pre-14th-century mosques, which undercuts the claim that Mansa Kanku Musa introduced architecture after his pilgrimage. Use as a caution in any Mansa Musa architecture claim.
- **note** (ch-007.txt chunk 4 (Ch 4 Dramani-Issifou)): Islam's outcome in Africa: the volume calls it a choice of society that became Arabised in north Africa, but in the rest of Africa Islam did not find the conditions it had in the east and north, and it advanced mostly through rulers who kept African traditions. Use in the overall Islam lesson as the volume's conclusion, stated as its view.
- **note** (ch-002.txt chunk 1 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): The Sudanic zone was never conquered by Muslims but was drawn into the Muslim economy by trade, and its main exports were gold and slaves. The volume says Islam entered the Sahara and Sudan along the trade routes and was gradually fitted into African ways of life. Use in the Ghana and Mali lessons as the volume's framing of Islam and trade, to be tested against the module's sources.
- **note** (ch-008.txt chunk 1 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): The Tuareg and Tin Hinan: Tuareg tradition traces the Kel Rela to Tin Hinan, a woman from Tafilalt who arrived on a white she-camel, and the Abalessa tomb excavations (1929 and 1933) match a fourth-century burial. The chapter flags a snake divination shared with a people al-Bakri describes near Ghana, and a link to Ghana as suggestive only. Use in the Tuareg and Sahara lessons, with the link marked as suggested.
- **note** (ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): The 'silent trade' may be a red herring: the chapter says the silent-trade story, widespread even beyond Africa, may have served to hide the real trade. Use in any Ghana gold-trade lesson: call the silent trade a story that the sources tell, not a verified method.
- **note** (ch-031.txt chunk 1 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Source figure to check: al-Bakri credits the Sanhaja king with over 100,000 thoroughbred camels for his army. This is a single source's figure and is probably exaggerated; attribute it to al-Bakri, not a count.
- **note** (ch-031.txt chunk 2 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Money: the Maghrib followed the gold-dinar system, while other regions used cowrie shells (from the Maldives), copper rings, salt bars and cloth. Bills of exchange and cheques existed in the Muslim world. The chapter calls the 'silent trade' of Herodotus a myth that dies hard (after Moraes Farias). Use in the trade lesson: drop the silent-trade picture.
- **note** (ch-031.txt chunk 2 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Trade and state formation: the chapter says trade was not the motive force behind the states of Ghana, Mali and the Almoravids; trade accelerated processes that grew from internal productivity. Many authors say the opposite. Present this as Bathily's position, with the rival view.
- **note** (ch-031.txt chunk 2 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Ghana's fall: the chapter's hypothesis is that Ghana's end at the close of the eleventh century came from internal conflict between a Muslim, trader-allied faction and a traditional, rural-allied faction of the ruling class. The chapter calls this a hypothesis. Use in the Ghana decline lesson with that attribution.
- **note** (ch-031.txt chunk 2 (Ch 27 Bathily)): Trade had mixed effects on states: it favoured political integration (Almoravid, Fatimid, later Mali and Songhay) and broke up earlier states (Ghana, Christian Ethiopia). Use as the course's summary of trade's political effects, with the examples given.
- **note** (ch-032.txt chunk 2 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Pottery carried across the Sahara: laboratory work (Louhichi) shows pottery was transported from Tunisia or Algeria to the Sahel. Use in the Sahara trade lesson as physical evidence of trade.
- **note** (ch-032.txt chunk 3 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Against the Islamic cause of cloth: raffia cloth, bark cloth and leather clothing were known in Central and savanna Africa, so the spread of cotton weaving is not simply a Muslim effect of combating nakedness. Use in the textile lesson as the counter-argument.
- **note** (ch-032.txt chunk 3 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Mats and carpets from Tunisia exported to the Orient from the ninth century; their technique is poorly known. Use in the North Africa export lesson.
- **note** (ch-032.txt chunk 4 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Central Africa: a regional commercial zone around the Copperbelt was in indirect contact with the Indian Ocean before 900, exchanging salt, iron, fish, raffia cloth, palm oil and red dyewood north to south. Interior East Africa shows no imports, which the editors find hard to believe, suggesting cloth and salt as the imports and rock crystal as exports. Use in the Central and East Africa trade lessons with this caveat.
- **note** (ch-032.txt chunk 4 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Summary: a good half of the continent was already in large-scale trade; Namibia and the Cape, the Liberian forest and the interior of East Africa were probably outside networks. The period was a starting point for the trade of 1000 to 1500, with regional networks subordinate to international trade. Use as the course's closing trade summary.
- **note** (ch-032.txt chunk 5 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): State or chiefdom in West Africa: the editors say the states of Gao, Ghana and Kumbi Saleh are well known, but Takrur's state existence is now clear; the Soso power of Sumaoro Kante (defeated by Sundiata in the thirteenth century) may be a state; Ife and Hausa and Yoruba states are open. Use in the Mali and Soso lesson, marking the state-versus-chiefdom debate.

### 2

- **refined** (ch-024 chunk 1 (Cerulli, Solomonic move south)): Cerulli: the Christian state moved its capital from Aksum to Lasta and later to Shoa's frontier, and the monastery of St Stephen at Lake Hayq was moved too; the Solomonid dynasty consolidated under Yekuno Amlak, and Sultan Sabr al-din of Shoa took refuge with the negus about 1277 to 1278. Module 2 Solomonic lesson can say the Solomonic move was a southward expansion against Muslim states.
- **extended** (ch-023 chunk 1 (Mekouria, Aksum after the 6th century)): Mekouria: Aksum's sea trade (Adulis) was cut by the Sassanid takeover of Yemen and rivalry with Byzantium; Beja (Zanafij) groups from the north pressed the Eritrean plateau and drove Aksum's kings south; Adulis was destroyed about the 8th century on archaeological evidence; coins name about twenty kings, from Endybis to Hataza, with Christian crosses on the reverse. Module 2 can explain decline with these causes rather than one collapse date.
- **extended** (ch-023 chunk 1 (Mekouria, the 10th-century queen)): Ibn Hawkal (c. 977) reports a queen who had governed Abyssinia for years after killing the king, and the History of the Patriarchs describes a queen of the Hamwiya who sacked Aksum and drove out the king, who appealed to Patriarch Cosmas and the Nubian king Georgios. Sources differ on her identity (a Falasha queen, a granddaughter of Wedem-Asfere, or Mesobe-Work's kin). Module 2 Zagwe lesson should mention this 10th-century crisis, labelled as contested.
- **extended** (ch-023 chunk 1-2 (Mekouria, Zagwe origins and churches)): Mekouria: the Agaw of Lasta, who had lived in the south-west for centuries, took power in the central highlands; the Zagwe dynasty's legend (Mesobe-Work marrying Mera Tekle Haymanot) is a romanticised version; Debre Damo's church (Axumite-style stone and wood, carved ceilings) is dated to about the 10th century, and about 120 rock churches around Guerealta may be 10th century or earlier. Module 2 can say Zagwe-era churches reuse Axumite forms, not that Lalibela's churches are Axumite.
- **extended** (ch-024 chunk 1-2 (Cerulli, Muslim states of the south)): Cerulli: Islamic states of southern Ethiopia were Damot (earliest), Shoa (Makhzumi sultans, from 896-7 until Ifat took it in 1280), then Ifat (Walasma dynasty, centre shifted to Adal by the 14th century). Sultan Sabr al-din I of Ifat fought Amda Seyon in 1332; Harar's emirate from 1520. Module 2 can list these states in the Ethiopia lesson, marked with the chronicle sources.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt chunk 1 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): Ethiopia after Islam closed the Red Sea: Islamic control of the Red Sea and its coast cut Ethiopia off from the sea and weakened the central state for two centuries, so the centre moved south, where the Christian revival began in the ninth century. From the tenth century Muslim merchants from Dahlak and Zeila moved into the interior and founded the first Muslim states in the south. Use in the Aksum and Ethiopia lessons.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Part II, Hrbek)): The baqt lasted about six hundred years: the treaty of AD 651-2 let the Nubian state of al-Makurra keep its independence, with rights of trade and travel and protection for Muslims in Nubia, and the Muslims chose a sphere of influence over conquest. It ended in 1315, when the Mamluks installed a Muslim king at Dongola and Nubia changed from dar al-harb to dar al-Islam. Use in the Nubia and Makuria lessons: the baqt's life and its end.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Part II, Hrbek)): Nubian Christianity's decline: Arab nomads moved into northern Nubia from the eighth century, and after the Mamluks interfered in royal strife the Nubian kings became puppets. Alwa, the southern Christian state, lasted until the early sixteenth century, when the Funj and Arab tribesmen overthrew it. Use in the late Nubia lesson, with Alwa's end dated.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Part II, Hrbek)): Ethiopia's Muslim trade: the Dahlak islands and Zeila were the two gates into Ethiopia, with Muslim merchants established in trade centres by the ninth century, though the Christian state forbade them to preach. Ifat, a Muslim state founded with a claim of Makhzumi descent, annexed Shoa in 1285. Use in the Ethiopia lessons linking Aksum's decline to trade.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): The baqt's terms, from al-Maqrizi: Nubia supplied 360 slaves a year to the governor of Aswan, the Arabs supplied 1,300 ardebs of wheat, 1,300 kanir of wine and linen and cloth, the Arabs would not attack Nubia, citizens could pass as travellers but not settle, fugitives were to be returned, and Nubia kept a mosque at Old Dongola. The chapter calls it a trade agreement as well as a truce. Use in the Nubia lesson with the figures attributed to al-Maqrizi.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): The Beja treaty of AD 831: after an expedition under al-Mu'tasim, the Beja leader recognised the Caliph's suzerainty and paid an annual tribute, while the Arabs gained rights to settle on Beja land, so the same kind of clause meant vassalage. Gold tribute later reached about 2,400 gm a year. The Nubian kings were drawn in: al-Hawqal says the Beja leader and King Georgios were taken to Baghdad. Use in the Beja and Nubia lessons on the dependency that followed the baqt.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): Old Dongola matches the sources: Abu Salih (early eleventh century) describes a large city with churches, large houses and wide streets, and a king's house with domes; the excavations since 1964 confirm this. A two-storey royal throne hall (about AD 700) was converted to a mosque in 1317. Use in the Nubia lessons on Dongola as the capital, with the excavated buildings named.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): Where the baqt slaves came from: the chapter suggests that Kordofan and Darfur, where Nubian-related languages are spoken and Christian pottery turns up, may have been the slave source, though it does not know whether slave-dealing was a state enterprise. Use in the Nubia and slave-trade lessons: the source of the baqt slaves is still open.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 2 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): Nubian economy: barter was the rule inside Nubia, with a customs frontier at Upper Maks (Aksha) separating the foreign-trade zone from the interior, and coins used only in the north. Exports were mainly slaves, with gold, ivory and skins. Use in the Nubia economy lesson: coins were for dealing with Egypt and Arabs, and the state controlled foreign trade.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 2 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): King Georgios's embassy to Baghdad (835): after the baqt arrears, Caliph al-Mu'tasim demanded payment; Georgios sent his son Georgios to Baghdad, where a revised treaty payable every three years was agreed, arrears were cancelled, and gifts were given. The chapter says some sources confuse the dates and that the king may have gone twice, once captured in 852. Use in the Nubia lesson on the second treaty, with the dates marked uncertain.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 2 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): Nubian military reach in the tenth century: in AD 956 Nubians raided Aswan, and in 962 occupied much of Upper Egypt as far as Akhmim, probably to help the Fatimids against the Ikhshidids. The occupation of Edfu continued after the Fatimid takeover of 969. Use in the Nubia and Fatimid lessons: Nubia's power was real and it chose sides in Egypt.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 2 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): Nubian succession: the throne passed in the matrilineal line, with parallel-cousin marriage common, so a son could succeed his father. The Queen Mother (nonnen, Old Nubian) had a court title, and a Queen Mother Martha is painted at Faras. The chapter sees an old Meroitic tradition of the king's mother's role. Use in the Nubia lesson on succession and the Queen Mother.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 3 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): Old Nubian writing: a Nubian language written in the Coptic alphabet with four extra signs. The earliest dated text is a graffito of AD 795 by the priest Petro at al-Sabu'a; the bulk of Old Nubian texts (saints' lives, a homily, prayer books, legal documents and letters from Kasr Ibrim) date from the mid-tenth century onwards. Use in the Nubia lesson on literacy: the Nubians wrote their own language from the eighth century.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 3 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): Nubian soldiers in the Fatimid army: Nasir-i Khusraw, who visited Egypt and Nubia in 1050, reports that the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir recruited Nubians into the army, rising to 50,000. The number comes from one traveller. Use in the Fatimid and Nubia lessons, with the figure attributed to Nasir-i Khusraw.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 3 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): Church architecture in three periods: the first used long three-aisled brick churches, the second brought stone cathedrals and central or cruciform plans in Dongola (the Church of the Granite Columns and the Mausoleum), and the third added domes around the late tenth century. A typical Nubian plan persisted in the north. Use in the Nubia architecture lesson.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt chunk 3 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): The Nubian golden age ended with the Ayyubids: Nubia's prosperity ran to the second half of the twelfth century, and after the Fatimids fell in 1169-70 relations with Egypt broke down, with armed encounters with Saladin's Ayyubid troops opening the Late Christian period. Use in the late Nubia lesson.
- **note** (ch-024 chunk 2 (Cerulli, k'at and Ethiopian Islam)): Cerulli: the earliest record of the use of k'at (Catha edulis) by Ethiopian Muslims is in the Ethiopian chronicle of Sabr al-din's war, about 1330s; Ethiopian Christian and Muslim armies both showed reluctance to hold conquered land. Module 2 can use this as an example of how the chronicles reflect the Muslim side.
- **note** (ch-011.txt chunk 3 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): Faras bishops and a possible Melkite takeover: two bishops held the see of Faras in 997-9, and the chapter explains the second as a Melkite, linked to the Fatimid caliph al-Aziz's Melkite favour, but says the evidence is debated. Use in the Nubia church lesson: the confession of a bishop is inferred, and the inference is contested.
- **note** (ch-011.txt chunk 4 (Ch 8 Jakobielski)): Nubian art is a local school: the murals combine Byzantine and Coptic elements into a Nubian style, with a distinct period sequence (violet, white, yellow-red, multicoloured). Use in the Nubia art lesson: name the styles and the Faras dating.

### 6

- **confirmed** (ch-002.txt chunk 3 (Ch 1 Hrbek) (agrees with ch-025 and ch-025 vs Ibn Lakis)): Africa and India 7th-11th century: this chapter confirms the earlier finding that there was no direct connection between East Africa and India in this period; al-Mas'udi says East African ivory went to India and China through Oman. Use in the Swahili trade lesson, with al-Mas'udi named.
- **refined** (ch-002.txt chunk 3 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): Chinese porcelain and coins on the East African coast mostly belong to after the eleventh century, so 'the history of East Africa written in Chinese porcelain' is an overstatement for this period. Chinese ships did not sail the Indian Ocean beyond the Malay peninsula under the Tang, and Chinese knowledge of Africa came through Muslim accounts. Use in the Swahili trade lesson: date porcelain by its period, not by the coast's whole history.
- **refined** (ch-029.txt chunk 2 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Peopling date: the chapter says the short chronology (peopling at the end of the first millennium) is now abandoned, and that people were in Madagascar well before 1000 CE in the regions surveyed; the 7th to 11th century period can no longer count as the start of settlement. Use this to replace any lesson line that puts first settlement around 1000 CE, but keep the uncertainty about how early.
- **refined** (ch-029.txt chunk 4 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Arab influence on Madagascar is overstated: the southern political and social structures resisted new influences, and the 'Arab' explanation has been applied too systematically to Malagasy culture. The chapter says that examination belongs to periods after the eleventh century. Use in the Madagascar lesson: avoid attributing early Malagasy features to Arab settlers.
- **contradicted** (ch-031.txt chunk 1 (Ch 27 Bathily)): East African trading centres: this chapter lists Pate, Kanbalu (Pemba) and Kizimkazi (Zanzibar) as Muslim trading centres, but chapter 25 (Domenichini) places Kanbalu in the Comoros or north-west Madagascar, al-Kumr. The two chapters disagree on the location of Kanbalu. State the disagreement, or use a neutral 'Kanbalu (location disputed)' in the East Africa lesson.
- **extended** (ch-024 chunk 1 (Cerulli, Dahlak and the Red Sea)): Cerulli: Arab raids on Ethiopia's Red Sea ports began early (Ethiopian raid on Hijaz 702); the Arabs destroyed Adulis and occupied the Dahlak Islands; a Muslim principality on Dahlak from the early 10th century took over Adulis's trade; over 200 Arabic inscriptions on Dahlak Kabir date 911 to 1539. Module 6 and module 2 can use Dahlak as the Red Sea counterpart to the Swahili coast.
- **extended** (ch-026 chunk 1-3 (Ehret, Early Iron Age Bantu expansion)): Ehret: by 600-1100 Eastern Bantu farmers were scattered across the Great Lakes, the coast, the Pare mountains and Mount Kenya; Bantu settled wetter lands with 900-1000 mm of rain, and yam cultivation remained important until late in the first millennium. Module 6 can present the Bantu settlement as a gradual, uneven spread into areas with few competing herders.
- **extended** (ch-026 chunk 3 (Ehret, Bantu banana and highland agriculture)): Ehret: highland planting agriculture (banana staple with irrigation and manure) took shape in the Pare mountains around 1000 CE, and the Chaga spread from there; bananas reached the Lakes from the south (Malawi and Zambezi) as well. Module 6 can give the Chaga case as one of several independent banana innovations.
- **extended** (ch-026 chunk 2-3 (Ehret, Great Lakes expansion and Bachwezi)): Ehret: Lacustrine (Rutara and Ganda-Soga) society expanded from the Bukoba area in the first millennium, with outward movement partly driven by forest clearance for charcoal. The Rutara expansion north-west near the end of the period is the start of the Bachwezi era, remembered only in later oral traditions. Module 6 Great Lakes lesson can use this as the origin of later kingdoms, not their founding.
- **extended** (ch-026 chunk 3-4 (Ehret, chiefship)): Ehret: a new chiefship emerged in the proto-Great Lakes society before the Common Era, with older petty chiefs relegated to religious and medical roles; control of iron smelting gave the new chiefs their economic base. Large cattle-based polities only appear after 1100. Module 6 can explain the Great Lakes kingdoms as later developments of this older chiefship.
- **extended** (ch-027 chunk 1 (Phillipson, Early Iron Age in central Africa)): Phillipson: by 600-1100 the Early Iron Age industrial complex covered central and southern Africa in an eastern and a western stream, with the western stream from Lower Zaire. Early Iron Age copper and mining at the Copperbelt and upper Lualaba drew trade over a wide area, and the Upemba cemeteries (Sanga, Katoto) show wealth by about 1000 CE. Module 6 can explain Kongo and Luba origins against this older base.
- **extended** (ch-027 chunk 2-3 (Phillipson, Later Iron Age break)): Phillipson: a sharp break in the pottery at about 1000-1100 CE separates eastern central Africa (Luangwa tradition, probably brought by whole families from north-west of the Copperbelt) from the west, where Early Iron Age traditions continued (Lungwebungu). Oral dynasties such as the Luba are later than the archaeological break: their political developments are dated to the 13th or 14th century. Module 6 should separate archaeological continuity from the traditions of kingship.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt chunk 1 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): East African coast in the Islamic network: the coast was part of the Muslim-run Indian Ocean trade, with exports of gold, iron and hides, and the Fatimids' trade with the Indian Ocean increased its role. The volume credits this trade with the flowering of Swahili culture in the next centuries, with Islam as a religion and culture spreading along with it. Use in the Swahili and Kilwa lessons as the Islamic context of the coast.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt chunk 3 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): The Waqwaq raid again: Ibn Lakis's account of the attack on Kanbalu (Pemba) in AD 945-6 is cited with the Chinese demand for tortoiseshell and panther skins. Use in the Pemba and Waqwaq lessons, with the raid cross-referenced to the Madagascar chapter's account.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt chunk 4 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): African iron to India: al-Idrisi (died 1154) reports African iron exported to India for steel blades. The chapter says Africa exported processed iron, probably pig-iron, not ore, because ore is too bulky for the vessels of the time. Use in the Swahili export lesson: Africa's exports were processed goods as well as raw materials.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt chunk 4 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): Waq-Waq as a term: Muslim authors used Waq-Waq for two regions, one south-west of the Indian Ocean (Madagascar and the coast south of Sofala) and one in south-east Asia, and al-Biruni places dark-skinned Waq-Waq islanders near lighter peoples, perhaps New Guinea or the Moluccas. Ibn Lakis's Pemba raid is best read as a Srivijaya expedition for African goods, bypassing the Muslim monopoly. Use in the Pemba and Waq-Waq lessons, with each reference read in its context.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt chunk 4 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): Srivijaya: a maritime power in Sumatra from the late seventh century, controlling the Malacca Strait and the spice trade, with contacts to China and South India, and Kalah as its meeting-port with Muslim and Chinese merchants. Use in the Indian Ocean lesson on the eastern side of the trade.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Part II, Hrbek)): Somali coast: Arab and Persian merchants settled Mogadishu, Brava and Marka, and Somali lineage traditions (Darod, Isaq) tell of Arab founders around the fourth to fifth centuries AH. The chapter says these are legendary, but the traditions reflect a period of intensive Islamisation and clan growth. The Somali kept their ethnic identity, unlike the Arabised Nile groups. Use in the Somali and East African coast lessons.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 4 (Part II, Hrbek)): Islam on the East African coast stayed a coastal religion: Muslim immigrants lived in closed communities in towns from Lamu to Mozambique, Islam did not reach the Bantu-speaking interior before the nineteenth century, and villages near Muslim towns were partly slave-raid victims. The society was Islamic but not Arabic: immigrants intermarried, and their mixed descendants spoke Kiswahili. Use in the Swahili lessons: Islam was a coastal identity.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 4 (Part II, Hrbek)): The Comoros and Madagascar: the Shirazi of the Kilwa chronicle are said to have settled Anjouan, and Muslims arrived around the thirteenth century. Their mixed descendants (the Antalaotra) spoke a Kiswahili dialect with Malagasy words. The Muslim north-west Madagascar towns traded, exported chlorite-schist vessels, and kept the sorabe script, but Islam never took over the Malagasy culture. Use in the Comoros and Madagascar lessons.
- **extended** (ch-029.txt chunk 1 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): The Darafify cycle: a Malagasy tradition of 'giants' (Darafify, Darofipy, Fatrapaitana) preserved in the Oslo A 6 sorabe manuscript (edited by Munthe, 1982). Their names are built from Austronesian, Sanskrit and Persian words for aromatics, spices, perfumes and medicinal herbs (murex dye, pink pepper, benjamin, incense, cinnamon). The authors take this as a hint that Madagascar joined Indian Ocean trade before the seventh century.
- **extended** (ch-029.txt chunk 1 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): The Darafify group is said to have controlled the east coast's aromatic trade (benjamin, cubeb pepper, Madagascar incense, cinnamon) from the far north to the Matatanana basin, with chlorite-schist working sites tied to them. Use in the Madagascar trade lesson as the trade-monopoly hypothesis, with the chronology flagged as unresolved.
- **extended** (ch-029.txt chunk 2 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Talaky and the south: a coastal and riverine site (Talaky on the Manambovo, Antandroy country) with fishing, export of smelted iron, hides and salted or smoked meat, and graphitised pottery; the sites were occupied until the sixteenth century, with a calibrated range of about 940 to 1310 CE, most likely the eleventh century. The oral traditions say nothing about these people. Use in the Madagascar south and exports lesson.
- **extended** (ch-029.txt chunk 2 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Metalwork: copper and iron ores were exploited, with traces of ancient mining, and copper work produced bracelets (vangovango). Words for copper in Malagasy (saba) and in continental Austronesian and Comorian are compared. Iron was smelted in the interior and exported through Talaky, which the chapter reads as the sea outlet for interior goods. Use in the Madagascar metal and trade lesson.
- **extended** (ch-029.txt chunk 2 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Network evidence: imported sgraffito-decorated pottery from Arabia and other unidentified imports, ivory pendants from Africa or Asia, and graphitised pottery that matches East African (Lelesu), southern African (Gokomere-Ziwa-Zhizo) and Champa (Sa-Huynh-Kalanay) traditions. The chapter reads Talaky as a transit point linking Madagascar to the South China Sea and the Mozambique Channel. Use in the Indian Ocean network lesson, linking to the Zhizo and Chibuene evidence.
- **extended** (ch-029.txt chunk 2 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Early seafaring: Chinese writers from the third to the ninth century describe Austronesian sewn-hull ships (kun-lun bo) about 50 m long, carrying 500 to 1000 people and 250 to 1000 tons of cargo. The chapter says Austronesian settlers may have arrived in outrigger craft late in the first millennium, but the first peopling cannot be tied to a date after the third century. Use in the Austronesian and Madagascar lesson.
- **extended** (ch-029.txt chunk 3 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Evidence for early Indian Ocean sea contact: the Periplus's sewn boats on the coast of Azania, the Ptolemy 'eating Ethiopians' of the south coast, Chinese kun-lun boats near Africa, banana cultivation from Southeast Asia in East Africa, coconut oil exported through Rhapta, and Cham slave traders. Use in the Indian Ocean contact lesson, sourced one by one.
- **extended** (ch-029.txt chunk 3 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Madagascar's trade value: its east coast had timber, aromatics and cinnamon-type products close to the African ports supplying Egypt. The chapter argues Calophyllum inophyllum (absent from Africa but present in Madagascar) shows Austronesians reached Madagascar before East Africa. Use in the Madagascar trade lesson with the plant evidence as an argument.
- **extended** (ch-029.txt chunk 3 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Islam and Madagascar: Malagasy seafarers who converted to Islam led Omani and Siraf sailors on the direct route to the north of the island, where the Onjatsy settlements remain; this was probably the case by the early tenth century. Al-Mas'udi's island of Kanbalu (mixed Muslims and idolatrous Zanj) may be in al-Kumr. Use in the Islamisation of the Indian Ocean lesson.
- **note** (ch-026 chunk 4 (Ehret, the interior and the coast)): Ehret: East African interior societies stayed small (dispersed homesteads, clan headmen, age-set institutions in the north), and trade did not penetrate the interior before 1100; the coastal trade of the 9th and 10th centuries was run by proto-Swahili, and Mapungubwe profited from Zimbabwe gold by the 11th and 12th centuries. Use with Module 6 as a caution against an interior-to-coast picture.
- **note** (ch-026 chunk 3 (Ehret, the Chaga and the Maasai age-set)): Ehret: Chaga age-set ideas probably came from Old Ongamo contacts, and the Thagicu generation sets have Nilotic inspiration. Age systems spread between neighbours, so they are not a single Bantu inheritance. Module 6 can mention this in its interior social-organisation note.
- **note** (ch-027 chunk 3 (Phillipson, language and archaeology)): Phillipson links the Eastern Highland Bantu languages (from a Shaba dispersal centre) to the start of the Later Iron Age in the east, and the western languages to the western continuity. He treats this correlation as tentative. Module 6 can note the correlation and its uncertainty.
- **note** (ch-027 chunk 1 (Phillipson, copper and foreign pottery)): Phillipson: foreign pottery at Roan Antelope suggests men travelled to the copper area to obtain metal, since potting was men's work; families did not travel for metal. Module 6 can cite this as a caution against assuming family migration.
- **note** (ch-002.txt chunk 3 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): The Indian Ocean was an ocean of peace for trade, though it had slave trading and large-scale piracy; the Muslim expansion did not stop trade because merchants avoided forced conversion. Use in the Swahili and Indian Ocean lessons on trade and violence.
- **note** (ch-002.txt chunk 4 (Ch 1 Hrbek)): Debuli and Indian arrivals: coastal oral traditions name the Debuli (Wadebuli), from al-Daybul, as arriving before the Shirazi. The date is disputed (before the towns converted, or with firearms, so late), and the only recorded man with the nisba al-Dabuli was installed by the Portuguese at Kilwa in 1502. Use in the origins lesson: an oral tradition needs a date and a document before it counts.
- **note** (ch-006.txt chunk 4 (Part II, Hrbek)): The traders-bring-Islam maxim fails on the East African interior: the chapter says the rule that Islam followed trade does not apply to south-eastern Africa, and the reasons are still to be investigated. Use in the Swahili lesson: flag this as an open question, not a settled pattern.
- **note** (ch-028.txt chunk 2 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Quote for the trade lesson: al-Mas'udi (tenth century) on the Zanj of Sofala, the gold of Waq-Waq and the Omani sailors carrying tusks to Oman, China and India. The chapter notes the Zanj did not use ivory themselves and wore iron rather than gold or silver. Quote this as a single attributed passage, not as a general description of the region.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 1 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Source limits for Madagascar before about 1000: written sources reach back only to the twelfth century; the chapter says the history of pre-1000 Madagascar is uncertain, with contradictory hypotheses. Oral traditions survive in sorabe (Arabic-Malagasy script) texts, in ritual texts, and in scattered collections. Use as the opening caution in the Madagascar section of the East Africa lesson.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 1 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Oral names as collective symbols: the 'giants' and 'dwarfs' (the Vazimba) are codes for prestigious or forgotten groups, not individual heroes; the same group may have other names at other times. The chapter sets aside the 'Arab settlement' tales, which were once taken literally. Use this in the source lesson on oral tradition as a warning against reading names as biography.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 1 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Cinnamon in place names: the Persian word darasiny (dar chini, 'cinnamon from China') survives in the north, and Ambodisiny (near the cinnamons) appears in the Darafify cycle. The chapter treats this as evidence of the Persian or Arabic-mediated trade in spices. Use as an example of linguistic evidence for trade, with the caveat that the chain of borrowing is argued.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 1 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Archaeological dates from the Madagascar sites (Lamboharana, Taolambiby, Ambasambazimba) are printed as about 730, 900 and 915 CE with error margins; the OCR is unclear, so verify the exact figures and margins against the printed page before quoting.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 1 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Zafi-Raminia: the chapter gives a proposed route from Sumatra to the Red Sea, India (Mangalore), and then Madagascar, as the Austronesian trader migration that the Malagasy traditions may reflect, and dates their arrival in the north-east after the late eleventh century. This is a hypothesis; present it as the authors' suggestion.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 1 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Chronology dispute: the short-chronology supporters (Poirier, Ottino, Verin) and the long-chronology supporters (Perrier de la Bathie, who proposed from five centuries to four millennia for the forest clearance) remain divided. The chapter does not settle it. Use as the course's example of an open debate.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 1 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Environment: the disappearance of large lemurs, the elephant bird (Aepyornis), giant tortoises and crocodiles around the start of the second millennium points to major human impact on the forest, with pierced teeth and pottery at sites of this period. Use in the Madagascar environment lesson.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 2 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Flora evidence: 86 per cent of Malagasy plants are endemic; Perrier de la Bathie counted 48 per cent of non-endemic plants as introduced by people, with 57.14 per cent in the windward region and 14.28 per cent leeward. The three percentages printed (57.14 + 14.28 + 28.75) sum to 100.17, so the last figure should be about 28.58. Do not quote the split without rechecking the source.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 2 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Carbon dates in this chapter (Talaky, Andaro, Andranosoa, Saradrano, Irodo) are given with error margins and calibrated ranges, sometimes unclearly in the OCR (for example Saradrano printed as about 490). Verify each date and its calibration against the printed page before quoting.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 2 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Madagascar's periwinkle (Catharanthus roseus) was used by sailors to reduce hunger and may have spread among sailors early; the Malagasy name tonga refers to this. Use as a small, sourced example of early plant transfer.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 2 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Historiography: the chapter says the history of Indian Ocean navigation remains unwritten, with the Arab-Muslim maritime expansion from the eleventh century overshadowing earlier navigations by Austronesians and other peoples. Use as a statement of the gap in the course's Indian Ocean material.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 3 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): The chapter's Austronesian hypothesis is a postulate: from surveys it assumes Madagascar was in the Indian Ocean trade by the start of the first millennium. The authors say so openly. Present the Austronesian-trade account as a hypothesis with its postulate stated.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 3 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Competing early dates for Madagascar's peopling: Miller puts it in the second millennium BCE; physical anthropologists give c. 550 BCE (Rakoto-Ratsimamanga) or a pre-Dravidian proto-Australoid origin (Fourquet et al., 1974). The chapter rejects these as outside its period. Use the spread of dates in the Madagascar origins lesson.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 3 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Aden and al-Kumr: after the seventh and eighth century disruption in South Arabia, people from al-Kumr (Comoros and Madagascar) conquered Aden in outrigger boats and made it their base; Ibn al-Mujawir says Arabs and Persians still needed three monsoons for the route in the thirteenth century. Use in the Comoros and Aden link lesson.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 3 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): The 945 attack on Kanbalu: the Arabic sources name the attackers Wak-Wak, and the chapter reads the raid as a clash between a Muslim-allied Malagasy fleet and a Kun-lun (Srivijayan or Southeast Asian) force guarding access to gold and metals, not a simple slave raid. The chapter says this is the authors' reading. Use with the Ibn Lakis account (slaves, ivory, tortoise-shell, leopard skins, ambergris) attributed.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 3 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Srivijaya and the straits: the Kun-lun world gained control of the straits after the Canton massacre of 878, making Malacca the terminus for ships to China. Use in the wider Indian Ocean lesson as the Asian counterpart of Madagascar's trade.
- **note** (ch-029.txt chunk 3 (Ch 25 Domenichini-Ramiaramanana)): Iron and Chams: a Cham tribute in 974 included forty pounds of iron, which the chapter uses to suggest southern Madagascar iron was worth fighting over. Attribute to Maspero's translation of the Chinese source.

### 5

- **refined** (ch-021 chunk 2 (Anquandah, Begho and Bono Manso)): Anquandah: Begho was a farming town from about the 2nd century CE and a trading centre from the 11th century, peaking in the 14th century (about 500 compounds, 5000 people); Bono Manso was the state capital that absorbed earlier chiefdoms around the end of the first millennium. Module 5 should separate the commercial centre (Begho) from the state capital (Bono Manso).
- **refined** (ch-022 chunk 1 (Andah, migration hypotheses)): Andah: the view that Upper Guinea peoples were driven to the coast from the interior (McCall from c. 5000 BCE; Correa from the 3rd century CE; Rodney from Sudanic political events) is popular but unproven. The course should state the drift model as one hypothesis among several.
- **refined** (ch-032.txt chunk 4 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Urbanism before Islam: towns existed in West Africa before the Muslim impact (Jenne-Jeno, Ife, Igbo-Ukwu, Benin, Begho, Kong, Nyarko on the gold edge, a town by the eleventh century); Kano, Zaria, Turunku and the lower Shari are named as likely proto-urban sites. Use in the Guinea coast and urbanism lessons: say that towns predated the Muslim trade in several cases, instead of treating towns as the trader's import.
- **contradicted** (ch-032.txt chunk 3 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Two iron ages: the old model of a first and second iron age, with the second beginning in the centuries of this volume, has been overturned by recent research. The chapter says talk of two distinct sequences should stop, and that dates vary by region. Chapter 25 and the course's earlier notes should not use the two-iron-age frame as a general rule.
- **extended** (ch-020 chunk 1 (Shaw, the spread of agriculture)): Shaw: the shift to farming in the Guinea zone was gradual, not a sudden switch. Early planting of wild grasses by fisherfolk, and of oil palms, moved in stages from gathering to planned production. Stone Age hunter-gatherer technology survived in places into the 11th century (Yagala, Sierra Leone). Module 5 can teach the gradual transition with this evidence.
- **extended** (ch-020 chunk 2 (Shaw, Senegambian megaliths)): Shaw: over 28000 dressed stones and 54 circles at Sine-Saloum are funerary; three carbon-14 dates fall in the 7th and 8th centuries. Explanations offered: iron wealth, or control of the gold trade from Bure and Bambuk; Shaw says the 8th-century date is early for Arab trade pull. Shaw also notes Kumbi Saleh's development from the 8th century as a gold collecting point. Module 5 can present the megaliths as an unresolved case of early wealth.
- **extended** (ch-020 chunk 2 (Shaw, Igbo-Ukwu)): Shaw: the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes (storehouse, burial chamber, disposal pit) were found by a man digging a cistern; wood from a copper-studded stool in the burial chamber dates to between the 8th and early 11th centuries. Eastern Nigeria had no copper or gold to export, so copper must have come by trans-Saharan trade or from elsewhere, and the find is disputed. Module 5 should flag the date and the import question.
- **extended** (ch-020 chunk 2-3 (Shaw, Marandet and copper)): Shaw: Marandet (Air, on the Gao-Egypt route) has about 42500 crucibles, dated 6th to 10th centuries; analysis of one residue showed copper, not gold. Arab writers report copper exported south from Sus, and a caravan of 2000 brass rods was dated to about 1100 in the Madjabat al-Kubra. Module 5 can cite copper as a trans-Saharan export to the Guinea zone.
- **extended** (ch-020 chunk 3 (Shaw, Ife and Yoruba urbanism)): Shaw: Ife's high point is the mid-12th to mid-15th centuries (by carbon-14 and thermoluminescence), so its apogee lies mostly after the period. Shaw proposes that trade and ritual centralisation grew together, and that the oni's wealth came from the trade in slaves, kola and horses. Module 5 can present Ife as a ritual and trade centre with contested sources of wealth.
- **extended** (ch-021 chunk 1-2 (Anquandah, Gold Coast 600-1100)): Anquandah: the Gold Coast 600-1100 is a formative 'dark age' with little documentation. Iron and proto-urban sites: Begho (earliest iron 105-255 CE), Bono Manso (smelting from the 4th century), Bonoso (660-1085), Nyarko suburb of Begho (965-1125), with pottery akin to ninth-century New Buipe. Module 5 can present the Akan area as an early iron-working and proto-urban zone, not an empty one.
- **extended** (ch-021 chunk 2 (Anquandah, Akan earthworks)): Anquandah: earthwork enclosures at Akyem Mansó and Akwatia, and at Oda and Abodum, are contested: defence versus labour camps for alluvial gold in the Birim valley. Defence is the stronger view but unproven. Module 5 should present them as contested.
- **extended** (ch-021 chunk 3 (Willett and Ife sculpture)): Anquandah and Ozanne: Ife's naturalistic brass and terracotta works date to about the 11th century on bronze dating, and Ife's bead and urban history begins about 350 CE with hamlets, then urban Ife. Bead links: segi blue glass beads from Ife match beads at Kumbi Saleh, Tegdaoust and Gao, a sign of contact. Module 5 can cite these bead links.
- **extended** (ch-021 chunk 3 (Connah, Benin walls)): Connah: Benin's linear earthworks delimit territory rather than defend it; the outer wall dates to the 13th century (tradition: Oguola) and the inner wall to the 14th or 15th century, which implies strong central government by then. Module 5 can use this to date Benin's centralisation as later than Ife's, with the tradition labelled.
- **extended** (ch-021 chunk 4 (Onwuejeogwu, Igbo-Ukwu and Nri)): Onwuejeogwu: Nri's state, sustained by ritual rather than force, dates to the 9th century, and Igbo-Ukwu may be the burial of a ruler in that system. Igbo-Ukwu's bronzes are leaded and not brass like Benin's, and the find is older than Ife's major bronzes. Shaw thinks copper came from trans-Saharan sources, but Onwuejeogwu cites copper at Abakaliki and Calabar. Module 5 should present both sources as open.
- **extended** (ch-021 chunk 5 (Allison, Akwanshi sculptures)): Allison recorded 295 hard-stone sculptures (Akwanshi) on the middle Cross River, about 500 km east of Ife, carved by Ekoid groups including the Nta and Nselle. Allison's four-to-five-century dynasty estimate is contested; the sculptures may date from the last centuries of the first millennium to the first centuries of the second. Module 5 can use this as an example of a regional stone tradition.
- **extended** (ch-021 chunk 5 (Anquandah, long-distance trade)): Anquandah: greenstone axes (from Bibiani) and kintampo rasps travelled hundreds of kilometres, and clay sources for pottery were up to 100 km away; he argues long-distance networks radiated from central points before the 12th century. Module 5 can use these as the Early Iron Age trade evidence, separate from the trans-Saharan trade.
- **extended** (ch-022 chunk 2 (Andah, Mande and Sapes)): Andah: Livingstone's sickle-cell argument dates early Mande movements to the 14th century and links rice and iron farming with them; Hair dates the Mande invasion to the 16th century and Lamp to the 15th; the 'Sapes' (Mel speakers) were earlier craftsmen; the Mande may have brought iron, cotton and warfare but not agriculture from nothing. Module 5 can set these dates side by side.
- **extended** (ch-022 chunk 2 (Andah, Senegambian megaliths and mounds)): Andah: the Senegambian stone circles (over 30000 square km, Dialloumbere with at least 54 circles) are burial grounds, probably of dynasties; excavations at Sine-Saloum date them around 1000 CE rather than the 14th century; over 4000 mounds with gold, carnelian and iron grave goods; the megalith builders were probably ancestors of present groups (Mandingo, Wolof, Fulbe). Module 5 can give the megaliths a 1000 CE date with a note on the disputed earlier date.
- **extended** (ch-022 chunk 3 (Andah, nomoli and pomtan)): Andah: nomoli and pomtan stone figures (in the thousands, Sherbro Island to Kisi country) date by association to the 6th-7th century at Kamabai, and Atherton and Kalous say they are an aboriginal Sapes product; Person (West Atlantic makers) and Andah prefer an independent local achievement, while Jenne-Jeno's terracotta is later (1000-1300). Module 5 should present the nomoli as an open attribution.
- **extended** (ch-022 chunk 3-4 (Andah, Vai and trade corridors)): Andah: Vai and Kono speakers moved to the coast as trade corridors formed (salt and dried fish moving north), not as a mass conquest; Hill argues that trade routes preceded population growth and more complex politics; Vai was adopted as a trade language. Module 5 can present the Mande spread as trade-led, labelled as a hypothesis.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt rapporteur's note (Ch 5 de Medeiros)): Iron in Africa is older: the rapporteur says iron was smelted by direct reduction at least five centuries BC in Nigeria, the Air region, Mali, Cameroon, Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi, with early iron in the Senegal bend, the Limpopo bend and Ghana from the first centuries AD. Use in the Nok, Taruga and Igbo-Ukwu lessons, with the newer dates given and the list stated as provisional.
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 3 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Copper and alloys: Igbo-Ukwu used a mastered copper metallurgy, with hammering, cold spinning, lost-wax casting (euphorbia latex replaced wax), and zinc, lead and tin alloys (tin probably from central Nigeria), and filigree work. The chapter says the old idea that copper technology came only from the north is no longer accepted. Use in the Igbo-Ukwu lesson (module 5) with these techniques named.
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 3 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Copper as currency: copper was a standard currency in Central Africa from 900; the Mauritanian, Air, Copperbelt and Phalaborwa sources supplied it. Copper and bronze were traded from the Sahara into the south. Use in the Central Africa currency lesson.
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 5 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Iron bells as a diffusion marker: single or double flange-welded clapperless iron bells; the single bell means military authority and the double bell kingship. The single bell is at Katoto in Shaba by about 1200 and the double bell in Zimbabwe in the fifteenth century, so the diffusion from Nigeria to Shaba was before 1200 and to Zimbabwe and Kongo before 1500. Use in the Guinea coast and diffusion lessons (module 5).
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 6 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Art south of the Sahara: the editors reject the old claim that nothing of African visual art survived; Nok, from the first millennium BCE, showed a long figurative ceramic tradition; the 'Upper Niger tradition' of ceramics, small metal objects and (at Bandiagara about 1100) wooden neckrests; Sintiu-Bara ceramic vases from the sixth century in Senegal. Use in the art and Guinea-coast lesson.
- **note** (ch-020 chunk 1 (Shaw, sickle-cell and malaria)): Shaw: the sickle-cell gene built up in populations that farmed in malarial areas, perhaps over 1500 years to the levels seen in north-eastern Nigeria; clearing forest for farms increased malaria, because of the breeding pools the farms made. Useful for a Module 5 note on disease and farming, labelled as a hypothesis.
- **note** (ch-020 chunk 3 (Shaw, slavery and Ife)): Shaw: the trade in slaves was probably the main export that paid for Ife's copper and brass; he suggests slave-raiding was harder in forest areas so buyers used local authorities. He cautions that not every bound figure in Ife art shows a slave. Module 5 should keep the slavery claim as a hypothesis.
- **note** (ch-020 chunk 4 (Shaw, northern influence on Ife)): Shaw: the guilloche and rosette patterns, impluvium houses and potsherd pavements resemble late Roman and Byzantine work, but he says these may be independent, and rejects the old Hamitic hypothesis. Module 5 can present these as cautious possible links.
- **note** (ch-021 chunk 3 (Dark, Benin chronology)): Dark: the Ogiso period's start is contested: Egharevba's court history and Dark's dating differ by about 130 years, and the first bronze heads in Benin date to the 14th century or earlier. Module 5 should give the chronology with both dates.
- **note** (ch-021 chunk 4 (Neaher, latex modelling)): Neaher: some south-eastern bronzes may be made by latex (rubber) modelling, which is recorded for Igbira, Tiv and Igala. Module 5 can mention the technical question as open.
- **note** (ch-022 chunk 3 (Andah, iron and farming in the Sierra Leone rock shelters)): Andah: at Kamabai and Yagala, iron-using levels date from the 7th or 8th century and stone tools continued to the 14th century; Liberia's rain-forest early Iron Age pottery resembles Zimbabwe's early pottery; rice, not millet or cotton, was the main crop in the Upper Guinea coast. Module 5 can cite these as evidence against a purely Sudanic origin for iron.
- **note** (ch-022 chunk 4 (Andah, conclusion)): Andah concludes the Upper Guinea peoples were active participants, with intensive agriculture, centralised monarchies, guilds and markets present before the Sudanic intrusions, and that iron and state life were not imposed from the Sudan. Use as a balanced conclusion for Module 5.
- **note** (ch-032.txt chunk 4 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Cultural spaces: the editors argue that before the eleventh century towns created cultural areas whose influence spread, which explains the spread of Mande, Yoruba and Hausa languages. West Africa was not a set of isolated ethnic villages. Use this as the course's framing for Guinea coast and Sahel cultures.
- **note** (ch-032.txt chunk 4 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Caste and bards: the editors say the most recent research suggests castes in West Africa were a recent development rather than ancient, and the bards in Sundiata's suite (thirteenth century) prove only that they existed when the traditions were fixed. Treat caste and bard claims in the course as a debate, not settled.
- **note** (ch-032.txt chunk 5 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Benin and Igbo-Ukwu: fortifications west of the lower Niger (the later Benin kingdom) show territorial struggle; east of the Niger there are no fortifications, which may mean either a territorial unity headed by Igbo-Ukwu or a different form of land use. Use in the Benin and Igbo-Ukwu lesson, stating the open question about the Igbo-Ukwu tomb.
- **note** (ch-032.txt chunk 5 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Sanga: the evidence points to slow evolution towards a chiefdom at Sanga, clearly established by the end of the tenth century; the spatial organisation of settlements in East Africa suggests collective rule under a kinship ideology, though this view has been questioned. Use in the East and Central Africa chiefdom lesson with the debate noted.

### 7

- **refined** (ch-028.txt chunk 1 (Ch 24 Huffman)): The old two-economy model (an Early Iron Age farming economy and a Later Iron Age cattle economy) is invalid: thick cattle dung at Zhizo and Toutswe sites in Botswana shows large herds, and the Zhizo herds on the Kalahari edge were as large as the later Leopard's Kopje ones. Economic variation reflects choices about environment and politics, not fixed cultural traditions. Use in the economy lesson.
- **contradicted** (ch-028.txt chunk 1 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Leopard's Kopje movement: some archaeologists treat the spread of Leopard's Kopje from about 1000 CE as one expansion of Bantu speakers from central Africa across the subcontinent. Huffman argues it was a northward move across the Limpopo (not south across the Zambezi), since its ceramics relate to Klingbeil and central Transvaal styles, not to Zambia or Malawi. Show both views, and say the course should take the northward reading as the more evidenced.
- **contradicted** (ch-028.txt chunk 2 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Origins of Zimbabwe culture: Huffman says the Zimbabwe Culture evolved from the Bantu Cattle Culture at K2 and Mapungubwe, so Mapungubwe is the first Zimbabwe capital, and its origins lie there, not at Great Zimbabwe. Other historians (Abraham, Garlake) argue the Mbire moved south across the Zambezi and built the kingdom through religious power. Present Huffman's view as the trade hypothesis and the Mbire view as the rival.
- **contradicted** (ch-032.txt chunk 3 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Mapungubwe spindle whorls: chapter 24 (Huffman, ch-028 chunk 2) dates them to about 1100, while this chapter (Devisse and Vansina) gives c. 900 for cotton at Mapungubwe and southern Mozambique and its footnote gives tenth and eleventh centuries for the Mapungubwe whorls. Give the range 900-1100 with the dispute noted.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt chunk 4 (Part II, Hrbek)): Swahili trade into Zimbabwe: Chinese and Persian ceramics of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries found in Zimbabwe show trade with Kilwa and Sofala, and in the fifteenth century Muslim merchants from Angoche and Mozambique traded with the Mutapa empire, where Portuguese records mention thousands of 'Moorish' traders. Use in the Great Zimbabwe lesson on the Indian Ocean trade reaching the interior.
- **extended** (ch-028.txt chunk 1 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Ceramic style as an ethnic marker: archaeologists in southern Africa use pottery style to trace Iron Age groups on three premises (style is made and passed on within groups, transmission is partly verbal, and same-style makers and users mean same language). Bantu-speaking groups are inferred from the ceramic continuum, which links to modern Shona ceramics. Use in the Iron Age lesson as the method, with the caveat that style and language need not match one-to-one.
- **extended** (ch-028.txt chunk 1 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Zhizo to Leopard's Kopje: the Zhizo people held south-western Zimbabwe, eastern Botswana and the northern Transvaal for about 250 years (700-950); their jars with stamped bands were replaced by Leopard's Kopje jars with incised triangles and loops, while the late Zhizo Toutswe settlements tripled. Many Zhizo chose to leave rather than join. The replacement of the Maxton people in northern Zimbabwe by Gumanye (eleventh century) shows the same northward move. Use in the Zimbabwe origins lesson.
- **extended** (ch-028.txt chunk 1 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Mixed farming evidence: early Iron Age sites sit in broken country where water, wood, soil and grazing lie close; sorghum, finger millet, bullrush millet and legumes are recorded at Zhizo, Toutswe and Leopard's Kopje sites; pottery shapes and grain bins show cultivation. Use in the Iron Age farming lesson with named sites.
- **extended** (ch-028.txt chunk 1 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Bantu Cattle Culture: a spatial pattern in which the men's court and cattle byre (with graves and communal grain pits) sit at the centre, with the huts of wives around it, and the sacred back of the settlement held most protected. Traced from historic settlements to Zhizo (tenth to seventh centuries), and found mainly among patrilineal Bantu who exchange cattle for wives. Use in the Zimbabwe settlement and society lesson, with the spatial pattern as evidence of a value system.
- **extended** (ch-028.txt chunk 1 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Shashi-Limpopo settlements: Schroda was the largest and most politically important Zhizo settlement; K2, six kilometres south-west, was the largest Leopard's Kopje settlement. Settlement size tracked political power. The area had broken sandstone soils, mopani woodland (elephant and ivory), and alluvial gold from the rivers draining the western Zimbabwe reefs. Use in the Mapungubwe and trade lesson.
- **extended** (ch-028.txt chunk 2 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Coastal trade reached the interior early: Schroda (ninth century) has the earliest substantial glass beads and ivory in southern Africa, and K2 more than all contemporaries combined. Coastal stations at Chibuene (near Vilanculos Bay, Mozambique), eighth to ninth century, yielded Islamic glass and Persian-type pottery, and blue beads matching the earliest in Zimbabwe. Use in the Indian Ocean trade lesson (module 6 link) and the Zimbabwe lesson.
- **extended** (ch-028.txt chunk 2 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Why trade wealth mattered: cattle had to circulate (loans, bride wealth) or the system broke, so they could not be hoarded; gold, ivory, glass beads and cloth were storable and came in large quantities, so hereditary leaders could grow very rich and use trade goods as bride wealth. Portuguese documents confirm the use of goods as bride wealth. Use in the politics and wealth section of the Zimbabwe lesson.
- **extended** (ch-028.txt chunk 2 (Ch 24 Huffman)): K2's court midden grew so large that by about 1020 it covered the central cattle byre, which was moved out, the first change in the Bantu Cattle spatial pattern. By about 1075 the midden stood nearly six metres high, and K2 was abandoned at that time as the capital moved less than a kilometre to Mapungubwe, which had two to three times the living space. Use in the Mapungubwe lesson with the midden as the measure of court activity.
- **extended** (ch-028.txt chunk 2 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Mapungubwe (1075-1220) as the first Zimbabwe capital: the king lived in a stone enclosure on the hilltop, elite were buried on the hill, royal wives had their own area, important men lived on the outskirts, and a three-tier hierarchy (commoner sites, hilltop district leaders, capital) is seen across the region. Chinese celadon was found in the king's area. Use in the Mapungubwe and class structure lesson.
- **extended** (ch-028.txt chunk 2 (Ch 24 Huffman)): Gold at Mapungubwe: by about 1150 gold objects were made locally, and a gold rhinoceros and a gold-sheet sceptre were found in elite burials; this is the first use of gold as a status symbol in the Iron Age of southern Africa. Spindle whorls from about 1100 mark the first cotton weaving in the interior, introduced by coastal traders. Use in the Mapungubwe craft and gold lesson.
- **extended** (ch-032.txt chunk 1 (Ch 28 Devisse and Vansina)): Bantu expansion: the editors date its end to about the sixth century; afterwards farming settled where climate allowed. In the Central African forest, shifting cultivation of yams, plantains and vegetables; in the savanna, two fields a year; further south, cereals and stock-raising. Cattle-raising in Botswana grew strongly after 800 and led on to the Khoi-Khoi's pastoral system in Namibia and the Cape later.
